expedition_metadata.user_query: If Congo, Zambia and Angola are so resource-rich, why are they still poor?

journey_deck.heading: Wealth in the ground, poverty on the surface
body_markdown: The numbers really are that stark. The DRC holds roughly 70% of the world's mined cobalt and enormous copper reserves, yet its GDP per capita sits near $650 a year. Zambia's copper is about 70% of its exports. Angola's oil has run around 90% of its exports.

So the puzzle isn't whether the resources exist. It's why turning a mountain of copper or a sea of oil into broad prosperity keeps failing. Economists have a name for this pattern: the **resource curse** — countries dependent on a single extracted commodity tend to grow slower, not faster.

journey_deck.heading: When copper or oil money floods in, what happens to the rest of the economy?

options.label: Farming and manufacturing boom alongside it
The currency strengthens and other exports become too expensive to sell
Nothing — one sector doesn't affect the others

reveal_payload.feedback_text: This is **Dutch disease**. A flood of export dollars pushes up the local currency's value, which makes everything else the country could sell — crops, textiles, manufactured goods — too expensive on world markets. The mine or oilfield thrives while the industries that actually employ millions of people wither.

journey_deck.heading: Extraction employs capital, not people
body_markdown: Here's the second gear. A modern copper mine or offshore oil rig is enormously capital-intensive: it runs on imported machinery, foreign engineers, and a small workforce. Angola's oil sector generates the bulk of national revenue while directly employing only a tiny slice of the population.

So the wealth arrives as a narrow stream flowing to whoever owns the concession — often foreign firms plus a domestic elite — rather than as wages spread across a workforce. Economists call this an **enclave economy**: a high-value bubble that barely touches the surrounding country.

journey_deck.heading: Why doesn't a booming copper mine automatically create mass employment?

options.label: Because extraction runs on expensive machinery and few workers, so most value flows to concession owners, not wages
Because mining is illegal to staff with local workers

journey_deck.correct_feedback: Exactly. The value is real but concentrated — it lands with owners and equipment, not with a broad payroll.
journey_deck.incorrect_feedback: Not quite — there's no law against local hiring. The issue is structural: extraction is capital-intensive, so a giant mine can produce billions in exports while directly employing very few people. The money exists; it just doesn't spread through wages.

journey_deck.heading: Money that doesn't come from taxing citizens
body_markdown: Now the political gear. When a government's income comes from selling oil or copper rights rather than from taxing its own people, the accountability loop weakens. A state funded by citizens' taxes has to keep those citizens reasonably satisfied. A state funded by a single export tap does not.

This concentrates the stakes: whoever controls the resource controls the country's cash flow. That's why resource booms so often coincide with entrenched elites, weak public services, and — in Angola and the DRC — long stretches of conflict fought partly over who commands the mines and wells.

journey_deck.heading: So is it the resources themselves — or something underneath them?

perspective_left.title: It's baked into the resources
perspective_left.summary: One camp emphasizes mechanisms that flow almost automatically from commodity dependence: Dutch disease, price crashes that wreck budgets overnight (Angola's economy contracted hard after oil fell in 2014), and enclave extraction. On this view, heavy reliance on a single commodity is itself the trap, whoever is in charge.

perspective_right.title: It's the institutions and history
perspective_right.summary: Another camp, associated with economists like Acemoglu and Robinson, argues resources are only a curse where institutions are already extractive — a legacy of colonial systems built to pull wealth out rather than build it in. Norway and Botswana got rich on oil and diamonds because their rules distributed and reinvested the windfall. Resources magnify the institutions they land in.

journey_deck.synthesis_payload: These aren't fully reconcilable, and serious economists still disagree on the weighting. What most now accept is that resources are an **amplifier, not a destiny** — they pour fuel on whatever institutional fire is already burning. The hard, unsettled question is how much a country can change its institutions while that fuel keeps pouring in.

journey_deck.heading: The wealth was never the missing piece
body_markdown: Put the gears together. Congo, Zambia and Angola aren't poor despite their resources — they're poor in a way that is tangled up with how those resources get extracted, sold, and captured. The commodity strengthens the currency, employs almost no one, funds a state that needn't answer to its people, and rewards controlling the tap over building anything else.

Botswana and Norway show it can go the other way. The deciding factor was never the size of the deposit. It was **whether the country's rules turned the windfall into wages, schools and diversified industry — or into a prize worth fighting over.**

payoff_layer.explain_it_back_prompt: In one sentence, how would you explain to a friend why a country can be full of copper or oil and still be poor?

branches.hook: How did Botswana get rich from diamonds when its neighbors didn't?
What actually is Dutch disease and where does the name come from?
How did colonial borders and extraction shape modern African economies?

mint_card.title: The Resource Curse
mint_card.shareable_synthesis: Resource wealth doesn't build prosperity or poverty — it **amplifies whichever institutions it lands in.**
